text: I always figured it's basically a big "don't wreck the science" move. If Cassini were to keep orbiting or drift around, it could eventually fall onto or fly near one of Saturn's moons, and that would contaminate the moon's environment with debris, chemicals or microbes from the spacecraft. For places like Enceladus, which might have liquid water beneath the surface, a crash could mess with the search for life, so the mission was designed to end by intentionally plunging into Saturn instead. It's less an option and more a safety net for the science.

Yeah, I get why that feels weird — you're not pushing with that leg, so it seems like it shouldn't hurt. But the leg that's "stationary" is still doing a lot of work. On a skateboard, even the planted leg has to stabilize your body, absorb small bumps, and keep you balanced, so it isn't just hanging there doing nothing. If your knee or ankle is taking too much direct pressure from standing in one spot for too long, that can definitely hurt, especially if you're also pushing off repeatedly.

I'd check a few things casually. One is whether you're favoring one side when you push, because the planted leg can get overloaded from the same impact pattern. Another is whether your stance is too far forward or back, which puts weird stress on the knee and shin. Also, skateboards don't have suspension, so small road vibrations travel straight up through that leg. If the pain is in the knee or around the ankle, it's usually from pressure, balance correction, or a slightly twisted position rather than from "not moving". A practical tip: make sure your feet are at least shoulder width or wider, and don't lock the planted knee completely straight, because that puts a hard load into the joint. If the pain is sharp, keep it short, and maybe try different board setup or softer wheels.

Pretty sure this trips people up because most black Americans have no memory of Africa, but the term Afro-American points to where the ancestors came from, not where people live now. It's about origin, not current residence, and that's the part that makes the question make sense.

Most of the enslaved people who were brought across the Atlantic came from regions of West and Central Africa, and even though generations passed, the label kept that connection. So it's like how some Americans still carry "Irish", "Italian" or "German" as part of their identity, even if they themselves never set foot there. It's a marker of heritage.

Well, mostly. Not every black American can trace direct roots to a specific African country, and the term is broader than any one place. Also, "African American" has sometimes been criticized as not fitting people whose families stayed in Africa and later immigrated, so you'll see debates about what the label covers. Still, the core reason it's used is to connect black Americans to Africa as an ancestral region, not to claim everyone actually came from there recently.

Yeah so I always figured it’s not that all drugs are bad, but the idea that intense pleasure with zero adverse effects is basically a fantasy, and for a pretty concrete reason. If a drug hits the brain’s reward system hard enough to produce that rush, it also changes the brain’s chemistry, and that change is the cost. Your brain doesn’t stay the same; it starts compensating, and that’s where the problems sneak in.

That’s how I understood it from what I’ve read and run into. The brain has this self-correcting system, and when you keep flooding it with a drug, it adjusts to handle the extra load. Over time that means you need more to get the same effect, or you feel pretty rough when the drug wears off. So the adverse effects aren’t some separate punishment tacked on; they’re part of the same process that makes the drug feel so good. It’s a bit like eating too much sugar for a long while: at first it’s a quick hit, but then your body and brain both start recalibrating, and the “zero adverse effects” version is the version you’d have to invent.

Also, even in a healthy person, drugs like cocaine or heroin don’t just give pleasure, they mess with things like sleep, heart rate, hormones, and mood. So “0 adverse effects” would mean no withdrawal, no tolerance, no weird side effects, and no long-term changes. That’s a lot of zeroes to pack into one drug. And once you add that the person can’t function without the drug anymore, it’s not really “0 adverse effects” anymore.

There’s another angle too: some people think “well, just take it in small doses,” and honestly that’s closer to the truth, but it’s not the same as the drug having zero downside. Small doses can reduce the hit, but the underlying chemistry is still there. It’s the difference between a car with the engine running in the garage and one actually driving on the road.

So my take is that the question is really asking for a magical exception, but the brain’s reward system isn’t set up for that. You can get pleasure without the crash sometimes, but “0 adverse effects” is the part that doesn’t really exist.

Hi Sam,

Yeah, buying a house is more confusing than it looks, but the process makes sense once you break it into stages. First, get your finances in order and get a mortgage pre-approval or, if you're paying cash, make sure your funds are ready. Then pick what you actually want in a home — bedrooms, location, size — and have a realistic budget. Don't start looking at houses without that, or you'll waste time on places you can't afford.

When you find a property, you'll usually put down a deposit after agreeing on price. That's when you need a solicitor or attorney. They handle the legal side, like the contract and title checks. You'll also want a building survey, not just the basic one. The surveyor will flag issues with structure, wiring, plumbing, or damp, and those findings can matter a lot for the final price.

Another practical tip: make sure any agreed changes get put in writing. Don't rely on verbal promises from the seller or their agent.

Cheers,
Alex

yeah, so what makes a 3-in-1 bodywash/shampoo/conditioner different from the individual ones? Honestly, the main difference is what's actually mixed into that one bottle. Instead of a formula built just for washing skin, or just for cleaning hair, or just for softening hair, a 3-in-1 has to include ingredients that try to handle all three jobs at once. That usually means milder surfactants and enough conditioning agents to soften hair, but without the dedicated strength of separate products. So you trade some performance for convenience. My take is that it's not really better or worse; it's just a compromise formula. If your hair is fine, or you have a specific scalp condition, the dedicated shampoo and conditioner will probably work better. But if your hair is normal and you want one product for everything, a 3-in-1 can be okay. I figured this out when I was using one for a while: it was easier, but my hair didn't feel as clean or soft as with separate products. At least that's how I understood it. If you've been having trouble, I'd try splitting them again.

Talk soon

Yeah, it basically comes down to GPS and satellite-based geodesy. A network of survey stations on the plate is monitored continuously or periodically with GPS, and the positions are compared over time. That gives you a velocity in millimetres per year. Satellites like GRACE or InSAR also help, and the numbers get checked against the geological record.

So you're not just watching one point move. You're measuring a whole frame of points, then seeing how the plate as a whole is translating. If someone asks how fast a continent is moving, the honest answer is: we measure that, and it usually comes out as a few millimetres per year, not metres. It sounds tiny, but it adds up over thousands of years.

That's the short version. If you want, I can send you a link to a good explainer on plate motion and GPS geodesy.

Cheers

inbreeding lowers offspring IQ mostly because relatives share more of the same genes, and that makes it likelier for both parents to carry the same recessive genes that affect brain development or cognition. In genetics terms, the key point is inbreeding increases homozygosity, which means an offspring has a much higher chance of inheriting the same recessive gene from both parents, and when those genes relate to how the brain develops or how the mind functions, they can show up more often. That doesn't mean every child of relatives will have low IQ, just that the risk goes up noticeably. Think of it this way: if two relatives both carry a quiet, hidden gene that weakens mental ability, their child is far more likely to inherit two copies, and that's where the average IQ drops. The science is less about a single "IQ gene" and more about the buildup of small hidden effects that show up together. In short, the lower IQ isn't some mysterious curse, it's the predictable result of relatives sharing genes and the recessive effects becoming visible in the offspring.

yeah so, I always figured it wasn't that the arm really does hurt less, but that it feels less because of how we think about it. An arm wound is in a place that's easy to see and treat, so it feels more manageable. You're not worrying about your chest or belly, and you can still use your legs to get around. There's also the fact that arms have a lot of nerves, so they do hurt, but people often expect a wound there to be less serious. With a hit, it's a dull ache or bruise that fades fast, and with a shot, you're dealing with one clear injury instead of the unknown danger of internal damage. At least that's how I understood it from what I've read, and it's why a stab in the arm can seem "milder" even though it still hurts plenty. Honestly, the mental relief of it being in a non-vital spot does a lot of the work.

So the short answer is that carbon monoxide is dangerous because it grabs onto your blood’s oxygen-carrier way more tightly than oxygen itself. Carbon dioxide, by contrast, is mostly a waste gas your body knows how to deal with.

When you breathe normally, oxygen from the air binds to hemoglobin in red blood cells and gets carried around the body. That’s how muscles, organs and the brain get the oxygen they need. Carbon monoxide does something a bit different. It binds to the same hemoglobin with about 200 times the strength of oxygen. Once it’s on there, oxygen has a hard time displacing it, and the blood’s ability to carry oxygen drops. That’s the core of why CO is so poisonous: it’s not really a toxic chemical burning your tissues, it’s more like it tricks your blood into carrying less oxygen than it should.

Carbon dioxide is the opposite end of the story. Your body constantly produces CO2 as a byproduct of metabolism, and your lungs are built to clear it out. Breathing in a bit extra CO2 doesn’t block oxygen transport the way CO does. In everyday terms, it’s less like a poisons-your-blood situation and more like a gas your body already handles as routine waste.

One thing that makes CO especially sneaky is that it’s colorless, odorless and tasteless, so you can’t just notice it. People often only get symptoms when oxygen delivery is already impaired, such as headache, dizziness or confusion. If you’re working near engines, heaters or poorly ventilated spaces, the practical tip is to make sure there’s good ventilation and never assume the air is safe just because you can’t smell anything.

Yeah so, the brace position isn't some magic pose that makes a crash safer on its own. What it does is get your body into a stable crouch that spreads out the impact. Your head goes down, arms crossed, hands hold your knees, and your feet stay planted. If you picture it, you're basically folding into a compact shape so the sudden stop hits your whole body instead of just your neck, head, or chest. That reduces the chance of whiplash, a broken collarbone, or organs getting jolted out of place. It's more about limiting movement than stopping the plane. You don't have to be a pro at this; the crew demo usually shows the basics, and you just copy what they show. If you're in a window seat, the rule of thumb is to face the wall, but the key is staying braced. It's a small habit with a big payoff.

Yeah so, a lot of old businesses were small, local shops, or trade guilds, and they were fragile. If the owner retired, had no heir, or a war hit the town, they simply closed. That's why you don't see many pre-industrial companies still around, even though some very old firms like De Beers or Ceylon Tea are famous. The industrial era changed things because companies got bigger, more standardised, and less dependent on one person or one town. That made some of them able to last for generations. So it's not that no old businesses existed; they just didn't survive into modern times, and the ones that did tend to be the global, industrial-era giants.

yeah, the whole thing feels less like a clear policy and more like 50 different rules stacked on top of each other. I always figured that the real headache isn't whether pot should be legal, it's that 24 states plus DC have it fully legal, 18 more have it legal for medical use, and the rest still make it illegal. You can be doing something perfectly okay in California and break the law in Texas, which gets weird the moment you travel. I've seen this a lot with people who drive between states, and it's not just a theoretical issue: your blood alcohol test doesn't tell you whether you're high, so the legal line is fuzzy. If I had to take a position, I'd say we should just make it legal everywhere or nowhere, because right now people are left to figure out which state's rules apply to them that day. That's the practical tip I'd give: if you use it, know the rules where you're actually standing.

I always figured my body isn't some little battery, but a chemical machine. The "electricity" people talk about comes from ions moving across cell membranes. Nerve cells push sodium and potassium around through tiny gates, and that movement creates a small voltage difference. It's more like a signal system than a power source. What amazes me is how fast the signal travels down a nerve.

I always figured sampling was just stealing bits of old records, but after poking around in a DAW and actually trying to chop a drum break, I started seeing why people do it. It’s not about replacing the whole song. Most of the time, it’s one small recognizable fragment that you lift into something new, and that’s what makes it stick.

When you sample an older song, you’re usually grabbing a few seconds of something—maybe a horn hit, a bass line, or a vocal phrase. You can time-stretch it, pitch-shift it, reverse it, or slice it into short pieces that don’t line up with the original groove. That manipulation is the point. If you left it as-is, it would sound like a cover, not a sample. You’re turning the source into a texture or a hook for a new song.

The practical side is what surprised me: you don’t just take the file and move on. If the sample is recognizable, you need the rights holder’s permission, or you can end up paying a fee or sharing royalties. There are short-usage workarounds, but they’re not always safe once a song goes viral. A lot of producers I’ve read about use obscure source material partly because it’s easier to clear. That’s a real part of the craft, not just an afterthought.

My take is that sampling works best when the fragment is so familiar that the listener’s brain instantly places it, then you twist it until it feels fresh. You can slow a fast break down, take a bright vocal chop and make it dark, or isolate a single note and loop it. The detail is in how you treat it. A raw two-bar loop from an old record, pitched down and buried in reverb, can anchor a whole track without anyone realizing they’re hearing that song at all.

One concrete example from my own experiments: I pulled a 1-second drum hit from a dusty soul record, reversed it, and used it as a reverse cymbal. It sounded nothing like the original, but the rhythm still carried that older feel. That’s the magic—recognition without direct quotation.

If you’re starting out, my tip is this: don’t sample the most famous 15 seconds. Pick a less obvious part, maybe a bridge or a horn tail, and spend time chopping and treating it until it stops sounding like the source. Sampling isn’t borrowing a song; it’s taking a piece of its history and making it do something it wasn’t originally doing.

Yeah so, honestly, the short answer is that your head hurts when you get a headache, and it can happen for all sorts of reasons. I always figured a headache is not just "my brain hurts." It's more that the blood vessels in your head tighten up or get irritated, and your nerves react to that. Sometimes it's the stress from work, or not sleeping well, or even a change in weather. I can't really tell if it's the tension in my neck that's driving it, but I've noticed it tends to build up after a day of hunching over a laptop. At least that's how I understood it. If I can, I try to catch it early, maybe with water, a short break, and moving around. That's usually enough, well, most of the time.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse, but afterward I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

Honestly I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

Overall I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

I paid $38 for the keyboard and kept it anyway, because of the switches. The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

When I asked the seller what the switches were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life—well, the under-21 version of it—so I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

First, the good: the circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view. That’s rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too—the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a “rip-off” way exactly, just... if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

And clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, there’s way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many “wow” moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing—more must be better—so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal—$99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

So about 2 years ago, we ordered 2 shirts for my dad from Rockmount Ranch Wear over the phone. They never showed up because the sales rep messed up the address on the paperwork: her handwritten "7" got read as a "1." The right address was 5407, but the box went to 5401. The people living at 5401 took it to the local UPS store to send it back. Then it just vanished, and nobody heard anything more about it. We didn't find out until a few weeks later. In the middle of arguing over it, we ordered another 2 shirts. Rockmount wouldn't refund the first 2. The owner got involved at that point. He admitted it went to the wrong address, but said no refund unless the shirts came back. He even said we were partly to blame for not being friendly enough to the neighbors at 5401, which was only 4 doors away. We challenged the original charge with our credit card company, and eventually got the money credited back.
